item.title: Why Every Patient Needs an AI Zebra Scan
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Why Every Patient Needs an AI Zebra Scan

AI's most confident answer may be its least complete one.

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • AI's confident answer may hide the rare condition it barely considered.
  • LLMs are built to narrow toward the typical, common answer.
  • Seeking the atypical clinical insight may add depth to the model.
Source: Image by Orna from Pixabay.

Medical students learn one of medicine's oldest lessons almost as soon as they step onto their clinical rotations. It's even become part of folklore and sound advice. When you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras.

Most patients have common diseases, and good clinicians learn to recognize familiar patterns before chasing unlikely ones.

But the counterpoint is also important. Medicine has always lived with a sort of tension between probability and possibility. Every experienced physician remembers a patient whose diagnosis arrived late, when everyone had accepted the first reasonable explanation and the zebra never got invited into the room. Interestingly, artificial intelligence may be creating a version of that same moment.

One Question, One Answer

More physicians are turning to large language models to support their practice—from data organization to clinical thinking. Most of those interactions follow the same path. A question goes in, and an answer comes back. The conversation often ends there—except for some conversational iteration, the model had said everything it had to say. But I'm not sure that assumption stands up to a little clinical and computational scrutiny. And I realize this can be a bit esoteric, but can also be important.

Large language models don't retrieve facts the way a textbook index does. One interesting variable behind how they generate a response is called temperature. Despite the name, it has nothing to do with medicine. It doesn't determine how deeply a model reasons. It determines how predictable its next word is. At low temperatures, the model sticks close to the most expected phrasing. At higher temperatures, it becomes willing to say something less obvious.

That's a modest and almost mechanical fact about language generation. But it produces an interesting side effect worth looking at. An LLM running hot will sometimes name a diagnosis that a model running cold never mentions at all. I don't think that means the model is reasoning more broadly. I think the model isn't reasoning more. It's just less guarded about what it says.

Most models default to a temperature near 1.0. That's the "factory setting" if you never touch the dial. ChatGPT's consumer interface runs cooler than that, closer to 0.7, which nudges it toward more typical, structured answers. Tools built for clinical or factual work tend to run cooler still, often well under 0.5, on the theory that consistency matters more than range. Nobody, as far as I know, is deliberately running a model hot for a second opinion that might conceive a deliberately wider variation and find a zebra.

Three Sweeps

That distinction is what got me thinking that maybe a patient deserves more than one pass at an AI's attention. Picture asking the same clinical question three times, and letting the model answer a little differently each time, on purpose.

A cold sweep stays close to consensus. Common diseases, familiar presentations, the cases a clinician sees every week. For most patients, that's exactly where the answer should end. The cost is equally clear, as the farther a disease lies from that center, the less likely a cold, careful model is to say it out loud.

A standard sweep loosens the grip modestly. Familiar diagnoses still lead, but less common possibilities start to compete for a mention. This is probably close to what most physicians already experience without realizing it, since few clinicians are thinking about temperature when they type a question into an LLM.

A hot sweep pushes further. Here the model may name uncommon diseases or even odd constellations of symptoms. Some of it will be noise. Some of it will cost a clinician added time for nothing. But every so often, this is where the diagnosis nobody was looking for gets said out loud, perhaps even for the first time.

Whose Job Is This, Really?

Here's the potential problem. None of this should require a physician to become a temperature engineer, running the same question through a model three separate times and then comparing notes. That's a burden nobody asked for, and it's exactly the kind of thing that gets a good idea dismissed as clinically impractical. The burden belongs to the system.

A differential diagnosis tool doesn't need to hide its range behind one confident answer. It could surface all three tiers natively, in a single pass. The system provides common diagnoses up top, a middle tier of reasonable alternatives, and a labeled set of lower-probability possibilities the model considered but didn't lead with. That range should come from how the system is built.

That's a design question more than a clinical one. Most of these tools are built to converge on the single most probable answer. And that's the same way a search engine converges on its top result. And it's important to recognize that while convergence feels like confidence, it can be far from complete. And somewhere in that gap is the zebra that goes unseen.

What Physicians Already Do

In many ways, physicians already build this range-checking into their thinking. A difficult case gets discussed with a colleague or presented at grand rounds. The patient's story rarely changes overnight, but what changes is the vantage point. It may be worth asking whether AI systems should be built to offer that same range on their own, rather than waiting for someone to think to ask twice.

I want to be careful here; this is a design proposition and not a clinical recommendation. Temperature is a clue I noticed, not a mechanism I fully understand. I don't know of any study showing that varying it, or structuring outputs around it, improves diagnostic accuracy or shortens the path to a rare diagnosis. As far as I can tell, this exact clinical interface hasn't been built.

Medicine has never trusted a single vantage point on a hard problem. Patients and clinicians ask for a second opinion, or perhaps a more eclectic perspective. Maybe the tools we're building should carry that same technological instinct.

Occam was right. The first answer is usually the most probable one. But today, medicine still needs to know what often disappeared beneath the clinical logic of the moment.

item.title: Why Do I Hate Pictures of Myself?
item.description:
Body Image

Why Do I Hate Pictures of Myself?

When the camera isn't the problem.

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • We often see ourselves through self-criticism instead of the camera's lens.
  • Confirmation bias can make photographs feel like proof of long-held beliefs.
  • We often overlook the memory because we're evaluating the appearance.
  • Changing how we see ourselves can change how we experience the very same photograph.

A friend sends you a group photo from dinner, a wedding, or a weekend trip. Before you've registered anyone else in the frame, you've already found yourself, and you've already found something wrong. The smile looks off. The face looks older than you expect. Your eye lands on the one part of your body you already have a complicated relationship with. Everyone else is texting back heart-eyes emojis. You're staring at the same photo, wondering whether no one else can see what you see, or they do, and are silently judging you.

Source: Photo by AllGo - An App For Plus Size People on Unsplash

If that sounds familiar, you're not alone in this, and you're not vain. You're doing something almost everyone with a body and a smartphone does. The real question isn't whether the photo is flattering. It's why you and the people standing next to you in it can look at the same image and walk away with such different reactions.

The Lens You Bring to the Picture

When you look at a photograph of yourself, you're not simply looking at the image. You're looking through everything you already believe. By the time a picture reaches you, it's already been filtered through years of history: body image, perfectionism, old comments from a parent or coach, weight stigma, and whatever your particular version of "not enough" happens to be. None of that is unbiased, and none of it stays out of the frame.

Psychology refers to this as confirmation bias, and it works exactly the way it sounds. If part of you has spent years believing you're unattractive, a photo doesn't get evaluated. It gets mined for evidence. The picture stops being a picture and starts becoming proof.

Why We See Ourselves So Differently

Most of us are far kinder to everyone else in a photograph than we are to ourselves. Notice what happens the next time someone hands you their phone and says, "Ugh, I look awful here." You're probably not looking at whatever they're criticizing. You're noticing that they look happy, or that the light was beautiful, or that you remember exactly where the picture was taken and how much fun everyone was having.

Yet when it's our own photograph, our attention narrows. The picture that makes a friend think, "Look how happy you were," makes us think, "My arms look terrible." It's the same image viewed through two completely different lenses. That difference is worth paying attention to because it reminds us that our reaction isn't an objective assessment of the photograph. It's an old story about ourselves that has become so familiar we mistake it for reality.

Source: Ian Dooley/Unsplash

When the Picture Stops Being About the Memory

At some point, many of us stop using photographs to remember moments and start using them to evaluate ourselves. Instead of asking, "Did we capture something worth remembering?" we ask, "Do I look acceptable in it?" Once appearance becomes the test every photograph has to pass, everything else—the trip, the people you love, the celebration, the actual memory—gets pushed into the background.

Ask anyone who's stumbled across a photograph they hated years ago. The picture hasn't changed. What has changed is their relationship with themselves. Many people eventually see what everyone else saw all along. Or, at the very least, they feel a pang of regret that they spent so much time feeling ashamed of how they looked instead of appreciating the experiences that photograph was preserving.

Looking at Pictures Differently

The next time a photo makes you flinch, try resisting the urge to treat your first reaction as the final word. Instead, ask yourself what was happening that day, who you were with, what you were feeling, and what you would notice first if this were a photograph of someone you loved instead of yourself.

This doesn't mean you'll suddenly love every picture of yourself. That's not the goal. The goal is to remember that your first reaction is one interpretation, not the truth. The lens through which you see yourself was built over a lifetime, and that means it can also change over time.

Years from now, you're unlikely to remember the thing you're criticizing today. You'll remember who was standing beside you, what made you laugh, and what that season of your life meant. Those are the moments photographs were meant to preserve, and they deserve far more attention than the impossible standards we've learned to measure ourselves against.

item.title: Guaranteed Ways to Make Yourself Anxious
item.description:
Anxiety

Guaranteed Ways to Make Yourself Anxious

How to recognize the ways anxiety fools you into staying stuck

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • Putting off doing things that make you anxious leads to worsened anxiety.
  • Labeling the experience of anxiety as traumatic makes it harder to cope.
  • Focusing on avoiding anxiety only makes you feel more scared and prevents self-confidence.
  • Focusing on the past reasons you became anxious is not the same as learning how to cope with anxiety.

You can find a lot of information about how to decrease your anxiety, but think about the things you accidentally do that guarantee your anxiety will worsen. I see my patients make consistent mistakes. Once you recognize them, you cannot unsee them.

  1. Focus on feeling peaceful instead of becoming competent in managing anxiety and panic anyplace, anywhere.
    Anxiety fools everyone into believing they are in terrible emotional or situational danger, even though they are not. No one can be in perfect control over when and how they feel anxious; a better goal is to become competent at living well even when anxious. Peace of mind can only be achieved once you know you can handle the worst-case scenario of anxiety without compromising your goals. For example, you continue to drive your children to their appointments despite fear of driving on busy roads, or you show up for a job interview and say what you need to say despite feeling panicked.
  2. Avoid people and situations you know will trigger anxiety or panic.
    Each time you avoid a situation or person who triggers anxiety, called negative reinforcement, you reinforce your tendency to get anxious and stay anxious. Each time you seek reassurance instead of trusting your judgment, you undermine your self-confidence. Wisdom dictates that you invest in your future with less anxiety by facing it now instead of putting it off. You will see that negative reinforcement is your worst enemy instead of the anxiety.
  3. Assume the things that led to your anxiety are what you should focus on rather than the maintaining causes.
    Understanding how you came to be an anxious person might be interesting and help you cultivate self-compassion; however, it is far removed from learning how to manage your anxiety in the present moment. Recovery from anxiety is about stopping the current cycle of being afraid of being anxious and learning how to be gritty in the face of anxiety. People who do not have anxiety disorders experience anxiety and occasional panic, but they categorize anxiety as an unpleasant and predictable experience that is normal and not to be feared. They remember it is more important to take risks and seek out discomfort in the pursuit of living well. They never wait to feel confident and calm before doing difficult things because they realize doing difficult things is what produces peace of mind and self-confidence.
  4. Label any anxiety-provoking event or person as traumatic instead of anxiety-provoking.
    Those who overcome anxiety learn the words they use have great influence over how they feel and act. They understand that words like trauma carry powerful associations with victimhood, loss of control, and loss of choice, and reserve them for things that are truly terrible and extraordinary, such as sexual assault, near-death experiences, and extreme physical and psychological pain. They label experiences that most people face, such as poor parenting, bad relationships, breakups, divorce, or near misses, as being distressing. They focus on what they can learn from difficult life experiences rather than the negative effects of such experiences. This helps them dial down the feeling of being victimized and normalize the difficulty of being human so they can more readily grow.

item.title: What Can You Learn From Your Indecision?
item.description:
Decision-Making

What Can You Learn From Your Indecision?

Wavering between two options does not mean part of you prefers each.

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • Indecision between close options doesn’t mean you secretly want to split your choice.
  • People rarely choose to randomize (say, toss a coin) on purpose, even when the option is free and visible.
  • People’s repeated choices rarely match their stated wish to split between options.

You are staring at two nearly identical apartments, or two health insurance plans, or two flavors of ice cream, and you cannot decide. Or maybe you are even torn between two suitors. You go back and forth and cannot settle. In an earlier post, I explained why this happens: Your brain is slower and noisier when two options are close in (subjective) value, a well-documented effect called strength of preference. But hesitation invites a tempting story. Maybe you are not actually undecided. Maybe some part of you wants suitor A and another part wants suitor B, and your wavering is that hidden preference leaking out, roughly in proportion to how torn you feel. My coauthors and I just tested this idea directly, in a paper published in Management Science, and the answer is reassuring: No, your back-and-forth is not a secret ballot.

The idea of a hidden vote

The notion is not far-fetched, and it has already been commercialized. A quick search of any app store turns up tools like Decision Maker & Chooser, Randomix, or Spin the Wheel, all built on the same premise: If you cannot decide, spin a wheel, roll a dice, or flip a coin, and let chance settle it for you. The implicit promise is that this is a shortcut to something you already wanted, just faster. It would also explain why people keep flip-flopping between two restaurants, two Netflix shows, or, yes, two suitors. Under this view, you are not making mistakes when you waver. You are running an internal version of one of those apps, a spinning wheel tailored to whatever split reflects your true taste, say, 70 percent for this one, 30 percent for that one, and your wavering just carries out that split imperfectly.

Putting the hidden vote to the test

To test this, 103 participants repeatedly chose between pairs of lotteries (small gambles with money at stake), some riskier but with higher prizes than others. Each pair repeated four times, with repetitions popping up randomly as the experiment went on. As expected, choices were more inconsistent across repetitions when the two options were closer in subjective value. Here, “subjective value” was measured separately and depends on your attitude towards risk. We then gave the same participants a chance to say, for each pair, exactly how they would want their four chances split between the two options: all four to one, three to one, two to two (in effect, a fair coin toss), one to three, or all four to the other. If wavering really reflects a hidden preference for splitting, a person's actual pattern of repeated choices should line up with the split that same person said they wanted, pair by pair.

It did not. Among the cases where participants stated a genuine wish to split their choice, the pattern of their repeated choices matched that stated wish only about 15 percent of the time. Wavering and wanting to split are correlated; both increase as two options get closer in value, but statistically, one does not predict the other well enough for them to be the same thing.

A trick for when you are stuck

Our second finding suggests a practical trick. When participants were given a costless, visible option to hand a choice over to an actual coin toss, they used it only about a quarter of the time, even for pairs where they were close to indifference. Most people simply picked one option and moved on. In a further experiment, we added a small, explicit cost to using the coin toss (from 10 cents to half a dollar), and the frequency of choosing it dropped sharply, to under 5 percent, even though the cost was often trivial next to what was at stake.

This suggests a trick for the next time you struggle with a decision. First, remember that the time you spend struggling is itself informative: It tells you the options are close enough in value that the choice barely matters. That time is also valuable, and you are wasting it. So just notice what you are leaning toward right now and go with it. If that does not settle things, imagine you had to pay 10 dollars for someone else to flip a coin and decide for you. Our participants faced a real (if much smaller) version of that cost, and overwhelmingly chose not to pay it. Ask yourself the same question. If paying to have someone else pick for you does not sound worth it, neither is the struggle. Pick.

What this means for you

Put together, these results paint a fairly reassuring picture. Your brain does slow down and grow noisier when considering two options that are close in subjective value. This is well established, and it is why agonizing over small decisions is often a waste of time (see the earlier post for concrete tips). What is new here is that this same struggle does not translate into a genuine, deliberate wish to split the difference. Most people, most of the time, would rather just decide, even when a free way to hand the decision to chance sits right in front of them.

So if you are torn between two nearly equivalent choices, or even two suitors, do not read your hesitation as evidence that you secretly want a bit of both, or that the right move is to alternate between them indefinitely. Go ahead and toss a coin, or open one of those decision apps, if that helps you move on. Just do not mistake the result of the coin toss for something you knew all along. Your indecision is telling you the options are close in value, not that you are running a hidden spinning wheel. Pick one option, and treat the tiny cost of “getting it wrong” as exactly that: tiny.

item.title: Sibling Rivalry or Sensory Rivalry?
item.description:
Neurodiversity

Sibling Rivalry or Sensory Rivalry?

How opposite sensory profiles can cause conflict in families.

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • Neurodivergent siblings often struggle with each other when their sensory needs are in conflict.
  • Meeting the needs of children with opposite sensory needs is difficult.
  • Openly discussing sensory needs helps normalize differences and empowers children to self-advocate.
  • Parents may also have opposite sensory needs from their children and should be mindful of their own self-care.

Early on in my therapy career, I was providing individual therapy to a pair of young siblings. Their mother asked if we could do some sibling sessions, explaining that their constant fighting at home was causing distress for the whole family. I asked a few questions, starting with, “Does this seem like typical sibling rivalry, or something more?” Their mother stated that it seemed like more than just the usual sibling squabbles, so I agreed to do a few co-sessions to observe what was going on.

Since the siblings already both knew me, they were pretty comfortable and began to fight early on in the first session. I focused on observing and taking notes, and had them come in a couple of times to ensure that my qualitative data was consistent. I brought mom and dad in for a parent session to follow up and told them, “I think I’ve identified the problem: Your kids have opposite sensory profiles.” I then explained to the parent what I had observed. One sibling was auditory seeking and constantly made noise. They banged toys together loudly, talked, sang songs, made silly noises, and seemed uncomfortable in the quiet. The other sibling was auditory avoidant. They would initially ask their sibling to be quiet, and when they didn’t quiet down, the second sibling became increasingly distressed until they blew up. This had happened repeatedly each time they had come in for co-sibling sessions.

Sensory Differences as a Source of Sibling Conflict Is a Common Occurrence

Source: Ron Lach / Pexels

Over the years, as I have focused on treating neurodivergent clients in my therapy practice, I have seen this scenario repeated over and over again: One sibling is hyposensitive and one is hypersensitive to certain categories of sensory input, which then leads to conflict.

This type of situation is difficult to navigate. Both children’s sensory needs are valid and related to their disabilities, but when one sibling’s needs are being met, the other’s needs are not. In other words, the sensory seeking child legitimately needs more sensory input, and the sensory avoidant child legitimately needs less sensory input. How are parents supposed to meet the opposite needs of two children at the same time?

So, What Should Parents Do?

While there are no easy solutions, here are a few things to try.

  • Talk about sensory needs. While you will need to ensure that conversations are appropriate for the child’s age and comprehension levels, many children, even young children, can understand their own sensory needs. Many can also understand that their sibling’s sensory needs are different. Talking openly about this will help normalize this concept, will help the children feel safe in expressing their needs, and will allow the children to be part of the process of finding ways to support each other.
  • Ensure that the children understand that their sensory needs are not a problem. Sensory input is something everyone needs. Some people need more input, some less. Make sure that each child understands that their needs are not a problem or a burden; they are just part of what is necessary for them to function, just like needing to breathe or eat.
  • If possible, set up a low-input sensory space. If a child needs quiet, dim lights, very little visual stimulation, etc., is there a space that they can go to with minimal sensory input? It doesn’t need to be a huge space. Many autistic adults, for example, myself included, find their closet to be a great low-input space to spend time in when needed.
  • If possible, set up a high-input sensory room. If a child needs a lot of sensory input, is it possible to set aside a place where they can go make some noise, have music playing, have bright lights, have plenty of visual input, etc? They may need space to move, so they will likely need a bigger space than their more avoidant sibling, but the space could be their room, the backyard, the garage, or anywhere they can get the input they need.
  • Create sensory bags. Get a bag, purse, backpack, or some other carrying case that each child can use when they’re on the go. Fill the bags with fidgets, headphones, sunglasses, and other sensory supports. Encourage the children to use their sensory supports when they need. Don’t forget to be proactive, rather than reactive, i.e., put the sunglasses on before the light becomes too overwhelming.

Kids Are Not the Only Ones Who May Be Struggling

Also, it should be noted that neurodivergent siblings usually have at least one neurodivergent parent. While sibling conflict over sensory input is usually more intense, parents and children can also struggle with each other’s opposite sensory needs. Don’t forget, as parents, to pay attention to your own self-care and sensory needs. It’s OK, for example, to take a break when possible if you are feeling overwhelmed, to wear headphones, to put on background noise that is acceptable to everyone, dim or turn on the lights, etc. While our children’s needs will often come first, that doesn’t mean we should ignore our own needs. All of the suggestions above can easily be adapted for adults in the house as well.

For neurodivergent families, talking about sensory needs and supports is a must and should be as common as talking about what’s for dinner. That’s the best way to get everyone’s needs met as much as possible. “Would you like your headphones during this lovely meal? Why, yes. Yes, I would, thank you!”
